title: Building sentences
examples: How do I know what the subject is?
Can I add more detail to make a sentence better?
What is the difference between simple and compound sentences?

explain.say: Today we learn how to build strong sentences.

items: Subject: Who or what does the action
Object: Who or what receives the action

explain.say: The subject tells us who is doing the action.
The verb is the action word in your sentence.
The object is the person or thing that gets acted upon.
Adding detail makes your writing much more interesting.

items: Detailed: The fluffy cat slept soundly.

explain.say: A simple sentence has one main idea only.

faq.q: What is the subject of the sentence 'The big dog chased the ball'?
faq.a: The subject is the big dog. It tells us who is doing the chasing.
asks: Who is doing the action here?
What is the doer in this sentence?

faq.q: How do I know if I need a compound sentence?
faq.a: You use a compound sentence when you join two complete ideas. You often use a joining word like 'and'.
asks: When should I use two sentences together?

faq.q: Is the object always a person?
faq.a: No, the object can be a thing, like a book or a toy. It is what receives the action.
asks: Can I write about an object that is not alive?

faq.q: What is the difference between a simple and a compound sentence?
faq.a: A simple sentence has only one subject and one verb. A compound sentence joins two simple sentences together.
asks: Are they just two sentences put together?
How many main ideas are in a compound sentence?

faq.q: If I change the subject, does the verb change?
faq.a: Yes, sometimes the verb must change to agree with the subject. This is called subject-verb agreement.
asks: Does the verb need to match the subject?
What if the subject is plural?

facts: A simple sentence contains one independent clause.
A compound sentence joins two or more independent clauses.
The subject performs the action shown by the verb.
Details can be added using adjectives or adverbs.

quiz.say: Identify the subject: 'The clever student answered the difficult question.'
quiz.why: The student is the one performing the action of answering.

wrong.0: This is the object, receiving the action.
wrong.1: This phrase describes what was answered, not who did it.
wrong.3: This is the verb, showing the action taken.

quiz.say: Which word correctly joins two complete thoughts: 'The rain fell hard, the streets flooded'?
quiz.why: We use a coordinating conjunction like 'and' to join two full sentences.

wrong.0: A colon shows a list or explanation, not a simple connection.
wrong.2: A semicolon is correct but 'and' is often easier for beginners to remember.
wrong.3: A comma alone is not strong enough to join two full sentences.

quiz.say: Which sentence is a compound sentence: A) The little bird sang sweetly. B) She read the book, and he watched the movie.

options.show: She read the book, and he watched the movie.
options.say: She read the book, and he watched the movie.

quiz.why: This sentence has two separate subjects and verbs joined by 'and'.

wrong.0: This is only one subject and one verb, making it simple.
wrong.1: This is also only one subject and one verb, making it simple.
wrong.2: This is also only one subject and one verb, making it simple.
